notes: Entirely fictional evidence-informed scenario, not a reconstruction or estimate of the excluded target cohort. Exactly 3,000 complete rows and six requested columns; unique synthetic IDs. All analysis variables continuous except recorded sex F/M; age is in years and lipids in mmol/L. No external individual records are used. Reproduce with generate(None, model_spec, seed). NUMERICAL EVIDENCE: Lee et al., Am J Hum Biol 2019, DOI 10.1002/ajhb.23199, PMC6435188 version 1 Table 1, rural Kenyan Luo/Kamba/Maasai: sex/group mean BMI 20.0-22.5, SD 2.6-4.8; TC means 3.6-4.0 mmol/L, SD 0.9-1.1; HDL means 0.9-1.2, SD 0.3-0.4. Retrieved methods: volunteer rural sample, original eligibility >=17, 2005 fieldwork, so not demographically representative of this request. Red meat consumption and its association with hypertension and hyperlipidaemia among adult Maasai pastoralists of Ngorongoro Conservation Area, Tanzania, 2020, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0233777, PMC7263614 Table 2: October 2018 survey, BMI 21.9 (3.9), TC 177.7 (38.9) mg/dL = approximately 4.60 (1.01) mmol/L using 38.67 mg/dL per mmol/L. These differing surveys establish a plausible range, not pooled calibration constraints. Kajiado Kenya 2020, DOI 10.3390/ijerph17196957, PMC7579460 Table 3: overweight/obese 39.7% men and 60.2% women, motivating a small higher-BMI town-transition component. Dyslipidemias and cardiovascular risk scores in urban and rural populations in north-western Tanzania and southern Uganda, 2019, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0223189, PMC6897412 Table 4: adjusted LDL overweight/obese differences +0.23/+0.48 mmol/L and HDL -0.06/-0.15 relative to normal BMI; female HDL +0.08. Discussion reports lower HDL associated with lower LDL but does not report the requested adjusted TC-HDL residual correlation. Christensen et al., 2016, DOI 10.3109/03014460.2015.1013987, PMID26073640 retrieved abstract: age positively associated with plasma cholesterol, men lower HDL; used qualitatively only. ASSUMPTIONS: 55% F; independent latent archetype probabilities 65% active pastoral, 25% settled rural, 10% town-transition, same for sexes and ages. Age 18-85 scaled Beta(1.35,3), independent of archetype and sex. Archetypes are illustrative environment/activity/diet summaries, not inferred participants or actual residence counts. BMI lognormal with specified sex/archetype means and SDs before truncation to 12-55; small age increase to 50 then decline. Lipid conditional arithmetic means are linear in age, sex, BMI and archetype; positive lognormal noise uses constant CVs 0.27 HDL and 0.28 non-HDL. TC=HDL+non-HDL; this biological component model naturally gives TC>HDL, but no TC-versus-HDL eligibility filtering, clipping or row deletion is used. Non-HDL is latent and not exported. Numerical slopes are modeling assumptions informed by, not equated to, categorical multivariable associations: HDL -0.012 and non-HDL +0.065 mmol/L per BMI unit; their sum gives within-archetype TC slope +0.053. Age slopes HDL +0.001/non-HDL +0.014 mmol/L/year. Reference is female aged40 BMI22 before group offsets. Group offsets and log-error correlation 0.08 between HDL/non-HDL are assumed. Shared HDL component induces positive TC-HDL residual correlation; its magnitude has no direct published calibration and is a major uncertainty. Marginal age/sex-adjusted BMI slopes include lifestyle-mixture confounding and are not constrained to the conditional coefficients. No post-generation coefficient matching, residual orthogonalization or sample standardization. Smoking, alcohol, infection, medication, pregnancy and measurement-error submodels are not separately represented; their heterogeneous effects are absorbed into archetypes and residual variability. These data support methodological exercises and sensitivity analysis, not causal or population-representative inference about real people. Preserve mmol/L; multiply fitted lipid slope by 5*38.67 for mg/dL per 5 kg/m^2. Trials assess generated data only.
